title: Acute change among chronic needs
stem: Four morning reports arrive together. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client with COPD whose usual exertional dyspnoea resolves at rest
A client with heart failure who is newly confused and cool with markedly reduced urine
A client with arthritis whose usual pain returns before the next prescribed dose
A client with diabetes who requests review of a recent dietary change
why: The reported breathing pattern is unchanged and resolves as usual.
New confusion, cool skin and reduced output suggest compromised perfusion.
Recurrent usual pain needs treatment but is less urgent than possible shock.
Dietary review is important but lacks an immediate deterioration cue.
takeaway: Prioritize acute multi-system deterioration over unchanged chronic symptoms.
learningObjective: Prioritize acute multi-system deterioration over unchanged chronic symptoms.

title: Assigning during competing urgency
stem: A nurse is assessing a client with new respiratory distress when a trained care provider asks about another stable client's scheduled weight. What is best?
options: Leave the distressed client to obtain the weight personally
Cancel the weight because one client is unstable
Assign the established weight task with reporting instructions
Ask the care provider to assess the distressed client instead
why: The stable routine task should not interrupt urgent qualified assessment.
The team can preserve routine care through appropriate task sharing.
The worker can complete the predictable task while the nurse addresses deterioration.
Acute respiratory assessment requires qualified clinical judgment.
takeaway: Use appropriate task sharing to preserve both urgent and routine care.
learningObjective: Use appropriate task sharing to preserve both urgent and routine care.

title: New bleeding during discharge
stem: A postoperative client awaiting discharge now has fresh drainage rapidly saturating the dressing and feels faint. What should happen?
options: Finish discharge teaching before seeking surgical review
Send the client home with instructions to call if bleeding continues
Ask transport to take the client directly to the follow-up clinic
Pause discharge and assess with urgent clinical escalation
why: Teaching should not delay assessment of possible significant bleeding.
The current change requires evaluation before a safe transition.
Routine transport is not the appropriate response to possible instability.
Rapid bleeding and faintness change discharge readiness immediately.
takeaway: New instability overrides a previously completed discharge plan.
learningObjective: New instability overrides a previously completed discharge plan.

title: Monitoring during off-unit test
stem: A client needs frequent neurological observations after a recent change. A routine off-unit test would interrupt monitoring. What should the nurse do?
options: Coordinate timing or qualified monitoring with the responsible team
Send the client and resume checks when they return
Ask the porter to perform the neurological observations
Cancel the requested investigation because monitoring is still needed
why: The team can balance diagnostic need with surveillance requirements.
An unplanned gap may miss further neurological deterioration.
The required observations need appropriate clinical competence.
The test may remain useful when timing and support are resolved.
takeaway: Preserve essential monitoring when coordinating investigations.
learningObjective: Preserve essential monitoring when coordinating investigations.

title: Urgent callback identity
stem: A nurse providing telephone triage hears that a client is alone and suddenly unable to speak clearly. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Establish the client's location and callback information
Arrange immediate emergency response according to protocol
Complete a lengthy routine history before escalation
Communicate the sudden onset information to responders
why: Location is needed to send effective help.
Sudden speech difficulty may represent a time-sensitive neurological emergency.
Lengthy history should not delay emergency activation.
Onset information informs urgent assessment decisions.
takeaway: Remote emergencies require location verification and timely escalation.
learningObjective: Remote emergencies require location verification and timely escalation.

title: Unmonitored message channel
stem: At a clinic visit, a client says they will send portal messages for any future severe breathing difficulty. The portal is reviewed only on weekdays. What should the nurse clarify?
options: Messages are safest because they create a written record
Severe symptoms need the urgent response pathway rather than an asynchronous message
Sending two messages guarantees immediate review
The client should wait for a reply before using another service
why: Documentation does not make a delayed channel appropriate for an emergency.
The response time must match the severity and urgency of symptoms.
Message volume does not change monitoring arrangements.
Waiting for an unmonitored reply could delay essential treatment.
takeaway: Match communication channels to the urgency of the problem.
learningObjective: Match communication channels to the urgency of the problem.

title: Virtual visit privacy setting
stem: During a video visit about sensitive care, the client says others can hear them and begins giving only brief answers. What is best?
options: Continue because the client initiated the connection
Ask them to type all details into the public chat
Offer a private time or suitable alternative communication arrangement
Ask the nearby people to answer on the client's behalf
why: Initiating contact does not establish adequate privacy for every topic.
Typing may still expose information through the device or platform.
An alternative permits fuller participation without unwanted disclosure.
Nearby people do not automatically have disclosure or decision authority.
takeaway: Check privacy conditions during virtual care, not only at booking.
learningObjective: Check privacy conditions during virtual care, not only at booking.

title: Generated note verification
stem: An approved documentation tool drafts a note stating that a wound was measured, although the nurse did not measure it. What should the nurse do?
options: Sign because the tool uses the standard template
Ask the next shift to measure later to support the note
Keep the statement if the wound appears unchanged
Correct the draft before signing and verify the remaining content
why: Automation does not transfer responsibility for accuracy.
Later care cannot make an earlier unperformed action true.
Visual impression is not a recorded measurement.
The signing nurse must ensure the draft reflects actual care.
takeaway: Verify generated documentation before taking responsibility for it.
learningObjective: Verify generated documentation before taking responsibility for it.

title: Unconfirmed staff credentials
stem: A newly hired worker is introduced as a nurse but their practice authorization has not been verified. What should the coordinator do before assigning regulated duties?
options: Complete the organization's registration and role verification process
Rely on the worker's previous hospital badge
Assign restricted duties while human resources checks later
Use the worker's stated experience as equivalent verification
why: Verification establishes the person's current authorized role.
An old badge does not confirm current registration or restrictions.
Unverified regulated practice may expose clients to unauthorized care.
Experience does not replace present practice authorization.
takeaway: Verify professional authorization before assigning regulated duties.
learningObjective: Verify professional authorization before assigning regulated duties.

title: Observer consent
stem: A client agrees to a dressing change but says they do not want a student observing it. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Ask the student to step out for the procedure
Treat consent to care as consent to any observer
Continue the agreed care respectfully
Make necessary treatment conditional on accepting the observer
why: The client's observer preference can be respected.
Treatment consent does not automatically cover all educational observation.
Declining observation does not negate consent to the dressing care.
Conditional access would exert inappropriate pressure.
takeaway: Distinguish consent to care from participation in teaching activities.
learningObjective: Distinguish consent to care from participation in teaching activities.

title: Unexpected loss of support equipment
stem: An outpatient's communication device fails during consent preparation. The client normally uses it to express detailed choices. What is best?
options: Ask the caregiver to answer every question automatically
Arrange an effective alternative communication method before relying on consent
Use nodding alone for all complex questions
Assume the earlier appointment booking establishes consent
why: A device failure does not establish incapacity or substitute authority.
Accessible expression is necessary for a meaningful decision process.
Simple nodding may not reliably communicate complex understanding.
Booking an appointment does not establish informed treatment consent.
takeaway: Restore effective communication before relying on a treatment decision.
learningObjective: Restore effective communication before relying on a treatment decision.

title: Transporting an unstable client
stem: A rural clinic client becomes unstable while waiting for a family member to drive them for assessment. What should the nurse coordinate?
options: An earlier family pickup without clinical support
A taxi with the referral note
An appropriate emergency transport and monitoring response
A later appointment after symptoms settle
why: Faster private transport may still lack necessary monitoring and treatment.
A taxi cannot provide emergency clinical support.
Transport capability should match the client's current instability.
Waiting for spontaneous improvement may delay essential care.
takeaway: Match transport level to current clinical needs.
learningObjective: Match transport level to current clinical needs.

title: Client reports unsafe home destination
stem: A client ready for discharge quietly says the planned destination contains a person who has threatened them. What should occur?
options: Keep the destination because transport is booked
Discuss the threat with that person before assessing safety
Ask the client to avoid conflict after arrival
Assess immediate safety privately and coordinate a safer transition
why: Booked logistics do not resolve a credible safety barrier.
Contacting the threatening person may increase risk.
Avoidance advice does not address the unsafe destination.
Private assessment and coordination can identify safer options.
takeaway: Include interpersonal safety in discharge readiness.
learningObjective: Include interpersonal safety in discharge readiness.

title: Goals after functional decline
stem: A client planned to return to independent cooking but develops a new dominant-hand weakness. What is the best care-planning response?
options: Reassess the goal, adaptive methods and available supports with the client
Keep the goal unchanged because it was originally agreed
Replace it with permanent dependence without further assessment
Wait until discharge day to see whether the hand improves
why: A changed function may require adapted means or revised goals.
An old agreement may no longer be achievable safely.
New weakness does not establish permanent inability.
Late assessment may leave practical support gaps.
takeaway: Reassess goals when function changes materially.
learningObjective: Reassess goals when function changes materially.

title: Coordinating a diagnostic preparation
stem: A client is scheduled for a test requiring fasting, but the meal tray arrives and a prescribed meal-related medication is due. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Verify the actual test preparation and timing
Clarify medication administration with the responsible team
Automatically omit all medicines for the day
Communicate the coordinated plan to staff and the client
why: The correct preparation may depend on the test and timing.
Fasting can affect safe medication use.
A blanket omission may interrupt essential treatment.
Shared information prevents contradictory actions.
takeaway: Coordinate test preparation with nutrition and medication needs.
learningObjective: Coordinate test preparation with nutrition and medication needs.

title: Escalation after unavailable clinician
stem: A nurse reports persistent severe new symptoms, but the usual clinician is off duty and has no immediate callback. What next?
options: Wait because that clinician knows the client best
Use the designated covering or emergency pathway for the current urgency
Call repeatedly without reassessing the client
Document the unanswered call as the completed response
why: Familiarity does not justify delaying needed assessment.
The available escalation route should match current clinical risk.
Reassessment and alternative escalation remain necessary.
An attempted call alone does not address the client's needs.
takeaway: Use covering pathways when the usual clinician is unavailable.
learningObjective: Use covering pathways when the usual clinician is unavailable.

title: Competing family caregiving roles
stem: Two relatives each believe the other will administer home treatments, and neither can explain the schedule. What should the nurse do?
options: Give each a copy and assume they will coordinate
Choose the relative who speaks first
Clarify willing responsibility and verify the practical plan before discharge
Ask the client to monitor whether relatives remember
why: Duplicate information does not resolve unaccepted responsibility.
Speaking first does not establish capacity or agreement.
A workable plan requires named responsibility and demonstrated understanding.
The client may still lack the needed care if roles remain unclear.
takeaway: Verify caregiver roles rather than assuming shared responsibility.
learningObjective: Verify caregiver roles rather than assuming shared responsibility.

title: Refused trainee performance
stem: A client permits a student to observe but declines having the student perform catheterization. What should guide the plan?
options: Observation permission includes performance permission
The student's learning requirement overrides the limitation
The instructor can consent for the client
Arrange competent care within the client's stated permission
why: Different levels of participation require attention to the client's wishes.
Education does not override a client's treatment choice.
An instructor does not replace the client's consent authority.
Care can continue while respecting the specific boundary.
takeaway: Respect the scope of permission for student participation.
learningObjective: Respect the scope of permission for student participation.

title: Critical information received by wrong team
stem: A home-care nurse receives a serious abnormal result for a client now admitted elsewhere. What is most appropriate?
options: Ensure timely communication to the responsible receiving team and confirm receipt
Assume the electronic system has forwarded it correctly
File it because the client is no longer at home
Ask the family to relay the result during visiting hours
why: Direct confirmed transfer prevents a potentially important result being missed.
Automatic routing may fail across transitions.
Changed location does not eliminate the need to route serious findings.
Family relay may delay or distort critical clinical information.
takeaway: Route serious results to the team currently responsible and confirm receipt.
learningObjective: Route serious results to the team currently responsible and confirm receipt.

title: Client participation in rounding
stem: A client says bedside rounds are too rapid to ask questions. Which changes support meaningful involvement? Select all that apply.
options: Ask beforehand what the client wants addressed
Use a planned pause for questions and understanding
Give all questions to family without asking the client
Arrange follow-up for concerns not resolved during rounds
why: Preparation identifies the client's priorities.
A pause makes participation practical rather than symbolic.
Family involvement should follow the client's wishes.
A named follow-up prevents unresolved concerns disappearing.
takeaway: Make room for client questions within team workflows.
learningObjective: Make room for client questions within team workflows.

title: Safety concern from family
stem: A family member says a usually talkative client is much quieter than normal; the recorded vital signs are unchanged. What should the nurse do?
options: Reassure because the vital signs are unchanged
Assess the reported change and compare with baseline
Wait until the family can identify a diagnosis
Record the concern only if another visitor agrees
why: Normal routine values do not exclude a significant behavioural change.
A familiar observer may detect deterioration not captured by standard measurements.
Families need not diagnose a change before it is assessed.
Independent corroboration is not required to take the report seriously.
takeaway: Use family observations as assessment information, not as a diagnosis.
learningObjective: Use family observations as assessment information, not as a diagnosis.

title: Interrupted consent teaching
stem: A client with decision-making capacity repeatedly falls asleep from exhaustion during a nonurgent explanation. What is best?
options: Finish the material because the full form must be covered
Obtain the signature during a brief awakening
Arrange a better time and reassess understanding before proceeding
Ask a visitor to repeat the final paragraph
why: Delivering information without effective participation does not establish understanding.
A momentary signature does not resolve fatigue-related comprehension.
Nonurgent timing permits a more meaningful conversation.
A partial repetition may leave the broader decision unclear.
takeaway: Time nonurgent information-sharing for effective participation.
learningObjective: Time nonurgent information-sharing for effective participation.

title: Unmet interpreter preference
stem: A client asks for an interpreter of a particular gender for an intimate examination. The examination is elective. What should the nurse do?
options: Explain that any available interpreter is equivalent
Proceed with family interpretation to avoid rescheduling
Cancel care permanently because the request is difficult
Explore an appropriate interpreter or timing arrangement with the client
why: Qualifications do not eliminate individual participation concerns.
Family interpretation may create additional privacy and accuracy issues.
A scheduling barrier can often be addressed collaboratively.
Elective care allows reasonable accommodation of the expressed need.
takeaway: Explore feasible communication accommodations for sensitive care.
learningObjective: Explore feasible communication accommodations for sensitive care.

title: Care plan contradicts precautions
stem: A rehabilitation plan includes group therapy, but the client has newly ordered transmission precautions. What is best?
options: Coordinate an infection-safe way to meet rehabilitation goals
Stop rehabilitation until every precaution is removed
Send the client because exercise is beneficial
Ask therapy staff to decide without sharing infection information
why: Collaboration can preserve activity while controlling exposure.
A blanket stop may create unnecessary functional harm.
Benefit does not remove transmission considerations.
The team needs relevant information to plan safely.
takeaway: Coordinate competing care goals through a shared safety plan.
learningObjective: Coordinate competing care goals through a shared safety plan.

title: Client record access request
stem: A client asks how to obtain a copy of their own care record. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Explain the approved access request process
Automatically print every third party's information in the chart
Verify identity through the required process
Offer help navigating the request pathway
why: The pathway supports the client's access rights appropriately.
Other people's information may require separate privacy consideration.
Verification protects against release to the wrong person.
Assistance can remove practical barriers to the request.
takeaway: Support client record access using verified authorized processes.
learningObjective: Support client record access using verified authorized processes.

title: Emergency supplies conflict
stem: A unit has one immediately available emergency suction unit. One client needs it for active airway secretions; another has a routine planned procedure. What should guide allocation?
options: Which client was booked first
Immediate clinical need with arrangements for the routine procedure
Which nurse has the longer assignment
Equal time regardless of clinical condition
why: Booking order does not outweigh an active airway need.
Priority allocation should address the immediate threat while preserving later care.
Assignment size does not determine this client's urgency.
A fixed split may leave the airway unsupported.
takeaway: Allocate urgent resources according to current threat and alternatives.
learningObjective: Allocate urgent resources according to current threat and alternatives.

title: Client-selected risk tolerance
stem: A capable rehabilitation client wants to practise a difficult transfer after understanding its risks. No assessment of the proposed method exists. What should the nurse do?
options: Refuse all discussion because any risk is unacceptable
Permit the attempt solely because the client accepts risk
Arrange a collaborative assessment and supported practice plan
Require the family to decide whether practice occurs
why: Care should consider meaningful autonomy as well as safety.
Risk acceptance does not replace competent assessment and support.
A structured plan can pursue the goal while reducing avoidable harm.
Family does not replace a capable client's choice.
takeaway: Support informed goals through assessed, proportionate safeguards.
learningObjective: Support informed goals through assessed, proportionate safeguards.

title: Team plan based on outdated baseline
stem: At conference, a discharge recommendation relies on last week's independent walking. The client now needs two-person assistance. What should the nurse do?
options: Let the meeting finish before mentioning it at discharge
Assume rehabilitation will correct the change quickly
Approve the plan because the baseline was documented
Present the current functional findings before decisions are finalized
why: A delayed correction can embed an unsafe support plan.
Improvement cannot be assumed without evidence.
Documented history does not override current function.
Current findings are essential to choosing a feasible destination and support level.
takeaway: Base transition decisions on current function rather than stale baseline.
learningObjective: Base transition decisions on current function rather than stale baseline.

title: Recurring missed observations
stem: A unit repeatedly misses scheduled observations during meal breaks. Which change most directly addresses the pattern?
options: Assign explicit qualified coverage for the observation periods
Remind clients to call if they feel different
Move every observation to the next full shift
Ask staff to remember which colleague is likely free
why: Named coverage addresses the recurrent responsibility gap.
Symptoms may not reliably identify changes needing observation.
Deferral changes the monitoring plan without clinical review.
Availability assumptions do not establish accountability.
takeaway: Use explicit coverage to prevent predictable monitoring gaps.
learningObjective: Use explicit coverage to prevent predictable monitoring gaps.

title: Consultation recommendation conflict
stem: A consultant recommends a plan that appears inconsistent with a documented allergy. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Clarify the allergy information and recommendation promptly
Implement first because the consultant is the expert
Communicate the concern with relevant reaction details
Confirm and document the resulting plan
why: A potential treatment conflict needs resolution before exposure.
Expertise does not remove the need to reconcile known contraindications.
Specific reaction details support an informed decision.
The clarified plan must be available to the care team.
takeaway: Verify specialist recommendations against client-specific safety information.
learningObjective: Verify specialist recommendations against client-specific safety information.

title: Patient partner in improvement
stem: A team redesigns appointment instructions after clients report confusion. What would add useful client input?
options: Ask only staff whether the wording seems clear
Test the draft with clients using realistic follow-up tasks
Count how many paragraphs were shortened
Choose the version with the most medical terms
why: Staff familiarity may hide problems experienced by clients.
Task-based feedback reveals whether the instructions support actual use.
Paragraph count does not establish comprehension.
Technical wording may make the instructions less accessible.
takeaway: Test care information with the people who must use it.
learningObjective: Test care information with the people who must use it.

title: Care transfer with equipment dependence
stem: A client uses an unfamiliar enteral-feeding pump. The receiving service confirms a bed but has not confirmed compatible equipment or staff readiness. What next?
options: Send the pump without explanation
Assume bed acceptance includes every technical capability
Verify equipment, supplies and competent support before transfer
Stop feeding indefinitely to simplify the move
why: The receiving team still needs a workable equipment plan.
Physical capacity does not necessarily establish technical readiness.
Verification prevents interruption or unsafe continuation of required care.
Unnecessary prolonged interruption does not resolve coordination needs.
takeaway: Verify the receiving service can deliver required technical care.
learningObjective: Verify the receiving service can deliver required technical care.

title: Health goal outside nurse expertise
stem: A client asks detailed questions about a complex benefits appeal affecting access to care. The nurse lacks that expertise. What is appropriate?
options: Provide a confident answer from memory
Tell the client the issue is unrelated to health
Ask another client who completed an appeal
Connect the client with qualified support while addressing immediate care barriers
why: Guessing may mislead the client about important options.
Financial access can directly affect treatment feasibility.
Another client's experience may not apply.
A suitable referral acknowledges limits while supporting access.
takeaway: Refer beyond nursing expertise without abandoning the underlying care need.
learningObjective: Refer beyond nursing expertise without abandoning the underlying care need.

title: Role clarity during rapid response
stem: During a rapid response, two staff both prepare the same intervention while no one records times. What is the best correction?
options: Clarify roles and confirm who will complete each essential function
Let both continue to show teamwork
Stop the response for a full staffing meeting
Assume documentation can be reconstructed from memory
why: Explicit roles reduce duplication and missed functions.
Uncoordinated duplication can introduce error.
A lengthy meeting would disrupt urgent care.
Memory reconstruction may lose critical sequence and timing.
takeaway: Use clear roles and closed-loop confirmation during emergencies.
learningObjective: Use clear roles and closed-loop confirmation during emergencies.

title: Client comprehension of referral
stem: A client thinks a specialist referral means the specialist will call today, but the service has a routine wait and no urgent symptoms are present. What should the nurse clarify?
options: The referral is completed so no further discussion is needed
Expected next steps, contact route and signs requiring earlier review
The client should call emergency services to obtain a faster appointment
All new symptoms should wait until the specialist calls
why: Referral submission does not establish that the client understands the pathway.
A practical plan distinguishes routine waiting from worsening symptoms.
Emergency access should be based on clinical urgency, not queue avoidance.
New warning symptoms may require earlier assessment.
takeaway: Explain what happens after a referral and when the plan must change.
learningObjective: Explain what happens after a referral and when the plan must change.

title: Uncertain home-care completion
stem: A home-care record shows a missed visit, but the caregiver says someone attended. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Verify which service attended and what care occurred
Assume the visit was completed exactly as prescribed
Assess whether any required care remains outstanding
Correct the record through the approved process once facts are known
why: Another visit may have involved a different task or provider.
Attendance alone does not establish prescribed care completion.
Current needs determine whether a care gap still exists.
Accurate correction preserves continuity and accountability.
takeaway: Verify the content of care, not just whether a visit occurred.
learningObjective: Verify the content of care, not just whether a visit occurred.

title: Professional feedback timing
stem: A colleague makes a nonurgent documentation omission that has been safely clarified. What feedback approach is most useful?
options: Raise it loudly during bedside handover
Discuss the specific omission privately with an improvement plan
Avoid discussing it because no harm occurred
Send a group message naming the colleague
why: Public criticism can undermine trust and disclose unnecessary information.
Specific private feedback supports learning after the immediate risk is resolved.
Near misses can reveal a meaningful learning need.
Group exposure may be disproportionate and unhelpful.
takeaway: Separate immediate safety correction from respectful learning feedback.
learningObjective: Separate immediate safety correction from respectful learning feedback.

title: Workload acuity mismatch
stem: Two nurses each have four clients. One assignment now includes two unstable clients while the other remains routine. What should the coordinator do?
options: Keep assignments equal because the numbers match
Ask the busiest nurse to skip documentation
Reassess acuity and redistribute qualified support
Wait until the next shift to compare workload
why: Equal counts do not reflect current nursing demands.
Essential documentation cannot simply be omitted to absorb unsafe workload.
Updated allocation should match actual acuity and required surveillance.
The current imbalance may require immediate support.
takeaway: Reassess workload using acuity, not client count alone.
learningObjective: Reassess workload using acuity, not client count alone.

title: Care plan after treatment refusal
stem: A capable client declines one proposed therapy but requests help with symptom control and mobility. What should the nurse do?
options: Suspend all care until the therapy is accepted
Record the refusal as the sole goal of care
Ask family to authorize the declined therapy
Continue agreed care and coordinate the implications of the refusal
why: Declining one therapy does not mean declining all nursing care.
The plan should include the client's remaining needs and choices.
Family cannot automatically override capable refusal.
Ongoing care can address accepted goals while the team reviews consequences.
takeaway: Continue appropriate agreed care after a specific treatment refusal.
learningObjective: Continue appropriate agreed care after a specific treatment refusal.

title: Documentation of uncertain cause
stem: A client develops a bruise after several transfers, but the cause is unknown. What entry is best?
options: Describe the bruise, assessment and reported history without asserting an unverified cause
State which staff member probably caused it
Omit the bruise until the cause is proven
Record it as pre-existing because the admission was recent
why: Factual uncertainty can be documented while necessary care proceeds.
Speculation may falsely attribute harm.
The clinical finding needs documentation regardless of known cause.
Recency does not establish when the bruise developed.
takeaway: Document findings and uncertainty without inventing causation.
learningObjective: Document findings and uncertainty without inventing causation.

title: Shared plan for recurrent crisis
stem: A client repeatedly attends urgent care because they cannot reach the usual service after hours. Which planning actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Identify a clear after-hours contact pathway
Tell the client to avoid all urgent services
Provide symptom-based escalation instructions
Check that the client can access the chosen pathway
why: An available contact can address problems before they escalate.
Some future symptoms may still require emergency care.
Specific instructions distinguish urgency levels.
A pathway is useful only if practically accessible.
takeaway: Make crisis plans specific, reachable and responsive to symptoms.
learningObjective: Make crisis plans specific, reachable and responsive to symptoms.

title: Competing needs in palliative care
stem: A dying client wants fewer interruptions and is comfortable; a routine nonessential assessment is scheduled overnight. What should the nurse do?
options: Wake the client because the form has a scheduled box
Review the assessment's purpose against goals and coordinate an appropriate plan
Stop every assessment without telling the team
Ask family to provide all clinical observations
why: Routine scheduling should be evaluated against the current goals.
The team can preserve necessary monitoring while reducing unwanted burden.
Unilateral cessation may miss essential comfort assessment.
Family support does not replace required professional observation.
takeaway: Match monitoring burden to current goals and clinical need.
learningObjective: Match monitoring burden to current goals and clinical need.

title: Repeated unexplained cancellations
stem: A client repeatedly cancels visits and finally reports the clinic entrance triggers memories of trauma. What is best?
options: Repeat the same attendance warning
Require detailed trauma disclosure before offering alternatives
Explore a workable location or approach with the client
Discharge the client from the service automatically
why: Warnings do not address the stated barrier.
Accommodation need not depend on unnecessary disclosure.
A collaborative alternative may enable needed care.
Automatic discharge leaves a potentially solvable access problem unaddressed.
takeaway: Use disclosed barriers to adapt care access collaboratively.
learningObjective: Use disclosed barriers to adapt care access collaboratively.

title: Receiving incomplete telephone report
stem: A transferring service reports only that a client is 'stable'; the client has a new oxygen requirement. What should the receiving nurse request?
options: A repeat of the word stable for documentation
Only the original diagnosis
Only the family's telephone number
Current respiratory findings, oxygen support and relevant trend
why: A label does not describe the current care needs.
Diagnosis alone does not establish present respiratory status.
Contact details do not supply the missing clinical assessment.
Specific current information supports safe receiving care and monitoring.
takeaway: Replace broad stability labels with current objective care information.
learningObjective: Replace broad stability labels with current objective care information.

title: Evidence applicability
stem: A unit considers a care protocol studied in independent adults for frail clients with cognitive impairment. What should be reviewed first?
options: Whether the population and care context support applying it here
Whether the protocol title sounds current
Whether implementation would reduce printed forms
Whether a vendor recommends rapid adoption
why: Differences in function and cognition may affect safety and effectiveness.
A current-sounding title does not establish applicability.
Administrative convenience cannot determine clinical suitability.
Vendor enthusiasm is not an appraisal of the local population.
takeaway: Assess evidence applicability before transferring a protocol to a new population.
learningObjective: Assess evidence applicability before transferring a protocol to a new population.

title: Referral feedback loop
stem: A referral was sent for swallowing assessment, but no plan returns and meals continue to cause coughing. What should the nurse do?
options: Assume the referral itself closes the concern
Reassess safety and actively obtain the assessment and interim plan
Wait for the next scheduled nutrition review
Document only the number of referral messages sent
why: Submission is not the same as completed assessment.
Ongoing symptoms require an actionable response and interim protection.
Routine review may not match the immediate swallowing risk.
Message counts do not establish safe care.
takeaway: Close referral loops by confirming assessment and an actionable plan.
learningObjective: Close referral loops by confirming assessment and an actionable plan.

title: Divergent discharge priorities
stem: A team emphasizes wound healing, while the client says inability to climb the entry stairs is the main barrier to going home. What should the nurse do?
options: Finish wound teaching and leave stair concerns for transport staff
Tell the client the wound is the only discharge criterion
Integrate access assessment into the discharge plan alongside wound care
Advise the client to stay on one floor after returning home
why: Transport staff cannot resolve every ongoing access barrier.
Discharge readiness includes practical function and environment.
Both clinical treatment and safe entry are necessary to a workable plan.
A restriction does not establish that the home can be entered safely.
takeaway: Combine treatment needs with the client's real-world transition barriers.
learningObjective: Combine treatment needs with the client's real-world transition barriers.

title: Declined support service
stem: A client declines a home service because the scheduled time conflicts with dialysis transport. What is the most useful response?
options: Record refusal without further discussion
Explain that service schedules cannot change
Ask family to replace the entire service
Explore timing coordination before concluding the service is unwanted
why: The stated barrier concerns timing rather than the care itself.
Possible coordination should be explored before assuming inflexibility.
Family capacity has not been established.
Resolving schedule conflict may make the recommended care acceptable.
takeaway: Explore the reason for a declined service before closing the referral.
learningObjective: Explore the reason for a declined service before closing the referral.

title: Safety plan comprehension
stem: A client can name the emergency number but cannot explain which symptoms require using it. What should teaching evaluation focus on?
options: Applying the plan to realistic symptom scenarios
Repeating the number until memorized
Asking whether the client feels confident
Obtaining a signature that information was received
why: Scenario application tests the decision the client must make.
Number recall does not establish urgency recognition.
Confidence may not match correct understanding.
Receipt documentation does not demonstrate usable learning.
takeaway: Evaluate recognition and action, not contact-number recall alone.
learningObjective: Evaluate recognition and action, not contact-number recall alone.

title: Shared professional concern
stem: Two nurses independently notice an unsafe handover gap recurring at weekends. What is the most constructive next step?
options: Wait for a harmful event before escalating
Present specific examples and propose a coordinated improvement review
Discuss only which individual was on duty
Have each nurse create a separate personal handover system
why: A recurring near miss can be addressed before harm occurs.
Concrete evidence supports a focused system improvement.
Individual attribution alone may miss the weekend process problem.
Separate personal systems can create inconsistent information and fail to repair the shared weekend process.
takeaway: Use repeated observations to improve the shared care process.
learningObjective: Use repeated observations to improve the shared care process.
